<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-author">Author</button></h2><div id="work-acc-author" class="accordion-collapse collapse show"><div class="accordion-body"><p class="mb-0 work-author"><a href="../poets/dandi.html">Daṇḍī</a></p></div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Kāvyādarśa covers a wide range of topics related to poetry, including its nature, purpose, types, and elements. One of the key concepts in Kāvyādarśa is Rasa, which refers to the emotional or aesthetic experience that a reader or listener derives from a work of poetry or literature. Daṇḍin identified nine primary Rasas, including Love, Humor, Pathos, and Heroism, and discussed techniques that poets can use to evoke these Rasas in their works. Another important concept in Kāvyādarśa is Alaṅkāra or ornamentation, which refers to the use of figurative language and other literary devices to enhance the beauty and impact of poetry. Daṇḍin classified Alaṅkāras into several categories, including Śabda (sound-based), Artha (meaning-based), and Samāsa (compound).<br><br>Kāvyādarśa is considered to be one of the most influential works on Indian poetics and literary criticism, and it has had a profound impact on the development of poetry and literature in India and beyond. Its analysis of Rasa and Alaṅkāra has been particularly influential, and continues to be studied and discussed by scholars today.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contents">Contents</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contents" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">In most printed editions, Kāvyādarśa work is divided into three chapters, with the exception of one, where the third chapter of the other editions is divided into two. Except for one, the majority of the printed editions have 660 verses. Daṇḍīn argued in Kāvyādarśa that the beauty of a poem stemmed from its use of stylistic approach, of which he identified thirty-six types. He was a major proponent of Guṇaprasthāna, the belief that poetry required qualities or virtues such as śleṣa (punctuation), prasāda (favour), samatā (sameness), mādhurya (beauty), arthavyakti (interpretation), and ojah (compassion). This poetry has the presence of one or more of these characteristics.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Kāvyādarśa is a unique and influential work on Indian poetics and literary criticism due to its comprehensive analysis of various aspects of poetry, including its nature, purpose, types, and elements. Its key contributions, such as the concept of Rasa and Alaṅkāra, have had a lasting impact on the development of poetry and literature in India and beyond, and continue to be studied and discussed by scholars today. Additionally, Daṇḍin's classification and analysis of literary devices and techniques provide a valuable framework for understanding and evaluating poetry, making Kāvyādarśa a seminal work in the field of literary criticism.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">The works of Daṇḍīn are known for its different styles, where many scholars have criticised it to be authored by different writers, while the quotes at the end of each prose proves to be written by Acharya Daṇḍīn himself. However, there are certain views that Avantisundarī is the head and Daśakumāracarita is the trunk of Daṇḍīn’s work. Since Daśakumāracarita seems to be the continuation of Avantisundarī, and both are available in fragmented parts, the views are appreciated by several scholars and students of Sanskrit literature.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-quotations">Quotable Quotations</button></h2><div id="work-acc-quotations" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">1\. रदल ि्मपि न्िेक्यं ््व्े दुष्टं ्थञचन। सय्द् ्विुः सुनदर्मपि श्श्वत्रेणन्े न दुभगार्म्॥ \[््व््दशगाः -१.७\] There should not be even the slightest useless or defective element in the composition, \[because\] it destroys all the efforts made. Just like white leprosy makes a beautiful body ugly.</div></div></div>
